This study introduces a novel method for detecting and monitoring structural damage in composites through electrical impedance tomography (EIT), which offers a cost-effective, real-time solution with a 3D visualization capability. A non-iterive approach to EIT reconstruction is employed, utilizing a neural network to convert measured impedance data into images. To evaluate an active active material known as the GIC, a strategy for detecting and locating damage is developed, and a genetic algorithm is used to determine the optimal configuration for the material. This algorithmic configuration for the in search of shape optimization is applied to determine the optimal configuration for the material in order to isolate and highlight areas of damage. Results from an experiment with a carbon fiber reinforced polymer demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in isolating and highlighting a 4mm diameter hole in a 100x100mm plate, and initial findings for damage shape optimization using the GIC are presented.

We're exploring whether combining simple components through convolutional neural networks (CNNs) truly results in a more capable system. Our hypothesis suggests that the complex interactions among CNN parts might actually introduce significant non-linearity, potentially rendering the system's performance incomparable to that of its individual components. To test this theory, we developed a straightforward, non-random CNN construction method and applied it to a variety of problems. Our findings reveal that while our proposed method offers several benefits over traditional CNN approaches, it also validates our initial concern that the system's performance isn't necessarily superior to its constituent parts in every scenario.

This work focuses on a tensor representation of Euclidean space, offering a detailed examination of the connection between geometric and tensorial approaches. The discussion encompasses various space entities, including vectors, scalars, and basis elements, and explores the utilization of metric tensors in raising and lowering indices. A comprehensive analysis of tensor operations, encompassing contraction, matrix multiplication, and the product with vectors, is presented. The work also investigates the properties of specific tensors, including the Kronecker delta and the metric tensor, and demonstrates how they function within matrix form calculations. A list of exercises reinforces the key concepts presented in this geoemtrically oriented tensorial framework.

The concept of "stealth" particles, which interact weakly with ordinary matter and thus evade detection in particle showers, has gained significant interest in recent studies. Although useful, this idea faces limitations due to its reliance on the "longevity" of heavy particles, a property that is highly improbable based on the "cosmic distance ladder" argument. In contrast, the "stealth" version of dark photons can enable certain types of "electro-weak" or "multi-TeV muon" scenarios with potentially reasonable dark sector parameter values, which may include axion-like particles. The current paper explores the "stealth" variant of dark photons in the context of the "multi-TeV muon" scenario, and also investigates an alternative "longevity" mechanism for heavy particles, rooted in the interaction between the dark sector and the neutrino sector.

The generators of global symmetries in Toda conformal field theories satisfy relations known as Ward identities. In the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, we prove that specific combinations of stress tensor combinations and first-order momenta operator derivatives are equivalent through their role in calculating correlation functions. This equivalence holds true even in the context of the first non-trivial contribution to correlation functions, indicated by the central charge's magnitude. These combinations correspond to integrated expressions that appear in the equation governing the calculation of three-point correlation functions' momentum dependence. This result contributes to a deeper comprehension of the properties of the stress tensor in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory.

It is established that reflection groups generated by Coxeter matrices are not bi-automatic. However, this exclusion applies only to infinite sets of reflection genes. When investigating the compact part of the reflection graph, it becomes apparent that free reflection groups have a bi-automatic structure. This contradiction can be resolved by understanding that the initial free groups have a distinct set of reflection genes with a finite conjugacy class. Consequently, it is now possible to generalize and extend this notion to high-dimensional generalization groups, including G/c_n, G/A_n, and the Coxeter labyrinth group L_n, demonstrating that they are also not bi-automatic in the broader context.

Recent advances in non-invasive brain-computer interfaces have made significant progress in identifying and counting steps from electroencephalogram data. However, this task remains largely unexplored using non-invasive electrocorticogram technology. In this research, we investigate the patterns in ECoG data that correspond to walking, as well as step rates, in ten subjects who walked while wearing an ECoG cap. We found clear differences in the frequency patterns of the desynchronized/delta power and the posterior alpha/β power between walking and standing still. In addition, we successfully estimated step rates from the ECoG data with high levels of agreement, ranging from 0.79 to 0.99. Our findings demonstrate that ECoG signals contain valuable information about movement patterns and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

Given a graph of finite vertices, we examine the group defined by a RAA group associated with the graph's presentations. Under specific conditions where this group preserves a RAA complex in a geometric way, we investigate the scenario where the RAA complex has a component that splits as a convex hull. Our findings demonstrate that if the RAA complex's decomposition contains a tree-like component of infinite extent, the group defined by the RAA presentation is not hyperbolic. Moreover, if the presentation is 2-compact, it is not CAT(-1)). Notably, if the RAA presentation defines a group that is not virtually commutator, it is also not hyperbolic.

Connectivity analysis is a fundamental aspect of complex systems research that seeks to uncover the interconnections between system components. Efficient computation of connectivity is crucial for dealing with large-scale, dynamic systems. We present a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity (DDEC) estimation, which leverages a generative adversarial network to accurately and computationally efficiently capture both within-variable and between-variable connections from limited data. DDEC simultaneously models connections in the frequency and time-frequency domains, providing a comprehensive and actionable connectivity estimate. We demonstrate the superiority of DDEC over existing methods in multiple real-world applications, including the analysis of stock market data, neural recordings, and gene expression data.

Determining movement in biological organisms from video footage is a complex task for both humans and computer systems. Biological movement perception involves numerous challenges, including an array of computational challenges. This report outlines some of these challenges and potential solutions, while also presenting a novel approach to address one particular issue. A potential application of this method is discussed, along with experimental findings. Furthermore, the article presents data gathered during an eye-tracking experiment associated with the problem it examines.

Higher Order Techniques (HOT) have been extensively utilized in optimizing iterative methods for solving large linear systems Ax=b, which arise frequently in various applications. These techniques facilitate convergence acceleration by transforming diagonal-free matrices A into diagonal matrices through variable redefinition and algebraic manipulation, thereby enabling significant performance gains when applied to iterative solvers for large-scale problems. Although HOT's effectiveness has been demonstrated for accelerating the Gauss-Seidel method, its potential to enhance modern sparse matrix techniques, particularly Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioning in Conjugate Gradient (CG) iterations, remains largely unexplored. This research investigates HOT's applicability to accelerate CG with GPU-accelerated BoomerAMG, revealing substantial performance gains of up to two orders of magnitude compared to the original CG/AMG method. Furthermore, our findings indicate that HOT's benefits are applicable to a wide range of iterative techniques, making it a versatile tool for optimizing CG iterations.

Our research examines topological Anderson conductors resulting from random binary disorders that cause a disorder-induced many-body localization transition in a one-dimensional periodic drive-kicked system. A constant DC electric field is applied perpendicular to the DC direction. When the strength of the DC field is high, a single-particle quantum Hall effect emerges, characterized by a non-zero Hall conductance. Conversely, a low field results in localisation and non-quantized Hall conductance. Our study of a high-field system with a gradually introduced random disorder reveals a non-zero integer Hall conductance in the presence of strong disorder-induced many-body localization and a zero Hall conductance in the weak disorder regime. A non-Abelian Hamilton-Wilberholt-Zhang (HZ) invariant is used to characterise this non-zero Hall conductance. When the field strength is lowered, the HZ invariant undergoes a sudden change, indicating a non-Abelian phase transition and a non-quantized value of the Hall conductance.

This study focuses on subobjects and their significance in mathematical structures. It begins by exploring cuts, defined as endofunctors that map objects to their specific subobjects, and examines properties of cut morphisms, which are functors relating distinct cuts of the same mathematical structure. The research then delves into a specific context, studying categorical structures as cut from a broad, superstructure, and discusses implications for more complex structures, such as signed categories from which orientable categories can be derived.

In the context of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, a scenario is examined where a complex phase in the mu term results in an inherently complex mass for one of the neutral Higgs bosons. A calculation method is developed to handle this complexity at a two-loop level, a requisite for a comprehensive understanding of on-shell produced Higgs bosons. A key finding emerges, demonstrating the necessity of applying a rigorous, complex-parameter approach to on-shell Higgs calculations, a task that perturbative expansions fail to adequately address. Consequently, precise, up-to-date two-loop approximations are essential for a reliable, quantitative analysis of this hypothesis.

This paper delves into the complexities of a novel contextual learning scenario,
where multiple agents operate within a non-stationary, decentralized context
bandit setting, featuring linear structures. We analyze two distinct
protocols designed to prevent a sharable configuration from hindering these
agents. The first protocol involves a leader-follower dynamic, where the agent
with the highest sum of past context norms controls the system setting, and we
achieve a total regret bound of $\tilde O(d^2\sqrt{T})$ for this protocol. The
second protocol is based on a distributed versioning control system, and we
obtain a total regret bound of $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T})$ for this protocol. Both
protocols are designed to allow agents to learn despite not having access to
their local context data.

We appreciate the discussion opportunities provided by Zeng, Wang, and Xu, as well as Li and Hu, which have been insightful. Our initial work addressed the DRTITR learning problem under distributional shifts, and in response to valuable suggestions from the discussants, three additional aspects were explored. First, building on Li and Hu's point, we examined and compared alternative resilience definitions, and investigated the relationship between our approach and traditional robust decision-making. Second, in response to Zeng, Wang, and Xu's suggestion, we developed a SREIT-based DRTITR algorithm that leverages additional data, and finally, we expanded upon our evaluation by conducting more extensive experiments.

A theoretical framework based on event shape engineering for heavy-ion collisions allows for the independent control of initial collision geometry and particle flow. This method is applied to investigate the relationship between flow and the initial phase of collisions in heavy-ion experiments. By analyzing LHC data from lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, we find that increasing the initial event geometry significantly influences the flow coefficient, even in central collisions where collisions are highly central. This effect is consistent with hydrodynamic predictions. Furthermore, events with a complex geometry lead to an increase in both average transverse momentum and transverse momentum variance. However, the influence of this effect on the study of flow is minimal. Consequently, event shape manipulation provides a valuable tool for enhancing the sensitivity to flow in searches for long-lived particles that decay into visible final state particles.

It has been universally accepted that in an extremal scenario with $K$ users in an interference network, binary power control can achieve GDoF extremal benefits over optimized power control, which is $\Theta(K)$ in dense networks and $\Theta(1)$ in sparse networks. In this work, we challenge these universal statements and prove that the extremal benefit of binary power control over optimal power control in dense networks is actually $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$, rather than $\Theta(K)$. Moreover, we confirm the existing extremal benefit of $\Theta(1)$ in sparse networks.

Integrating fluid dynamics equations using a particle-resolved approach presents significant computational challenges, particularly due to the need for highly refined spatial and time discretization near particles, which can lead to complex and restrictive numerical schemes. To address this issue, this study introduces an innovative method that leverages physical particle-particle collision frequency to determine time step sizes, combined with a multiple time step integration approach to improve computational efficiency. The proposed method simplifies boundary treatment by decoupling near-particle and far-field discretization, thereby relaxing spatially varying time step restrictions. To demonstrate the method's capabilities, a 2D rigid particle-fluid interaction model was implemented, showing improved computational efficiency compared to existing models while maintaining accurate simulations.

This article presents multiple solutions to find integer solutions for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ for any positive whole number $n$. By leveraging properties of the Gaussian integers, a fundamental characteristic of the number 7 in unique factorization, and a specific property within the ring of integers of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$, we establish that this equation has its own set of infinite integer solutions, which can be expressed using coefficients of the ternary expansion of $(1-\zeta^2)^{11}/(1-\zeta^4)^3$ in $A=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$.

This project focuses on developing a novel monoped that navigates through air by hopping, utilizing a single leg consisting of one actuator and two passive joints. The hopping mechanism relies on the monoped's inertia and the elastic properties of the ground it hops on. Initially, a mathematical model was created to simulate the monoped's behavior in the air and on the ground, incorporating its inertia and the ground's elasticity. The model was used to determine the optimal size and actuator force for a 1-meter-long monoped, resulting in a design that could hop 40 centimeters with a 20 Newton force. The design was then built and tested, and various strategies were explored to enhance its hopping distance, including adjusting the actuator's timing and adjusting the angle of the foot's joints. The monoped achieved the greatest progress when the rear joint's angle was modified, allowing it to hop 1.2 meters over air.

A novel approach to QCD hadron structure analysis is proposed, centered on flexible meson form factors. This approach uses complex variables to generalize meson properties, enabling a connection between different hadron parameters, such as the charge radius, pion and sigma pole positions, and vector meson masses and masses of other particles. By fitting a simple two-parameter function to experimental data, we find a unified representation that yields consistent results across various hadron parameters, including the correct pole positions for vector mesons and particles, and a flexible meson mass range.

Graph clustering methods aim to partition networks into groups of related nodes, with hierarchical representations offering a more detailed and flexible alternative to flat clustering results. Historically, computing these hierarchical structures has been a time-consuming process, particularly for large-scale networks. This paper presents two innovative frameworks that efficiently generate hierarchical clusterings by breaking down the complex task into manageable sub-problems. The first framework, known as the linked representation, organizes the graph into a set of interconnected components, each responsible for a specific cluster, and achieves near-linear performance on various network types. In contrast, the second framework, called the acyclic representation, structures the graph as a set of overlapping clusters arranged in a tree-like format and demonstrates superior performance on specific network genres. To showcase the practical value of these frameworks, we integrate them into the ClusterEngine software, which is demonstrated through a range of cluster validation metrics and real-world applications, including enhanced web page organization and image retrieval improvements.

We investigate the optimal duration for quantum annealing to achieve a quench and obtain a high-quality final state in a quantum-annealed exact cover problem. A 2D array of numbers has an exact cover if we can select non-overlapping numbers that sum to $10^{20}$ in each row, column, and diagonal. Our study comprises two main components. First, using numerical methods on random generated instances, we determine the quantum annealing interval for two quench dynamics scenarios: obtaining a RCP close to 1 and an excited state near the ground state. The quantum annealing interval is found to be approximately 100 units for the first scenario and 10000 units for the second. These results are validated through numerical simulations of R production. Second, we investigate quantum quench dynamics in an exactly solvable RPP model, showing that the R production probability is directly related to the square of Bessel functions. This allows us to estimate the quantum annealing interval as 100 times the initial R frequency for production of R's close to 1, and 10000 times the frequency for production of R's near the lowest RPP state.

We employ Hubbard model calculations to investigate the effects of thin-film screening on the electronic behavior of infinite-layer nickelate superconductor. By examining multiple degrees of screening, including the growth of a surface oxide layer and variations in sample quality, we found that the degree of electron doping changes by up to 10 percent. This in turn affects key parameters of the model, including those responsible for the superconducting characteristics. Our analysis suggests that highly underdoped or even nodeless d-wave pairing could be present in this material.

A key aspect of dense stellar matter is its elasticity, which is characterized by the speed of sound. In neutron stars, the relationship between density and elasticity is a primary factor in determining their internal structure. To investigate this, we derived a consistent model for dense matter that accounts for quark interactions, including the effects of strangeness, and used it to calculate the speed of sound in dense matter. We then examined the absolute maximum speed of sound in this model. Furthermore, we used a statistical analysis of theoretical models to establish a prior distribution for the speed of sound in these models. We found that the prior distribution is closely linked to the properties of nuclear matter and that the parameters of the Quark Mass Model can be inferred from the compact star mass-radius data.

All-younger-older-older ( younger \ older )  states are well-established in quantum optics and atomic physics, with their characteristics defined by interference patterns and particle distribution. State types, including initial-younger (initial \ older) , are also established, with unique interference patterns and application potentials. Here, we introduce a new type of state, the initial-compass (initial-compass) state, with properties influenced by both phase interference and compressional effects, resulting in four state types with distinct features. Through simulation and experimental means using compressed cat states as initial-compass states, we demonstrate their distinct patterns and versatility. This flexibility allows for unique applications in continuous-variable, high-dimensional, and non-separable Hilbert space scenarios.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a powerful mechanism that drives rapid gas mixing in protoplanetary disks, and its intensity is believed to contribute to the suppression of planet formation near the snow line. To better understand this phenomenon, we investigated how the VSI evolves over time as the dust within the disk influences its behavior. By 200 days, we found that VSI-driven mixing can deplete the disk of millimeter-sized particles, and this depletion of particles can then impact the VSI's intensity, potentially delaying planet formation by reducing the amount of gas that can be mixed. We found that VSI-driven mixing is most effective in outer regions of the disk where millimeter-sized particles dominate, and this effect can be modeled using a simple dust evolution framework that incorporates V�. -driven mixing as a dry landslide process. As the VSI depletes the disk of millimeter-sized particles, it paves the way for smaller particles to migrate inward and eventually form planetesimals. To better understand this process, we developed a more comprehensive disk evolution model that incorporates the VSI's impact on particle mixing and particle mixing's impact on VSI. By 10,000 days, we found that VSI-driven mixing can clear a dust-depleted zone in the disk and that the VSI is most effective in the disk's outer regions where millimeter-sized particles dominate. These results suggest that VSI-driven mixing can delay planet formation by clearing

This research focuses on a specific class of positive solutions to the Liouville equation within an n-dimensional space, particularly those solutions where the gradient of the function's square is constant. To achieve this, we developed a new technique to derive a lower bound for the function's square and subsequently applied it to derive polynomial growth estimates for harmonic functions of degree zero on shrinkers with uniform properties. Notably, in the scenario where the dimension is two or greater and the uniform distribution of scalar dimensions is present, we found that bounded harmonic functions are equal to their constant forms.

Malicious updates that force a model to misclassify samples into a specific target class, despite correctly classifying other inputs, are known as evasive backdoors. Traditional backdoor research primarily focuses on models trained on static data, whereas our work examines more challenging scenarios where malicious updates are designed to exploit a model's learning of general patterns, making detection through traditional methods difficult. In our investigation into non-trivial erasing backdoors that function effectively in open-world settings, we aim to force a model to misclassify images into a particular target class when specific content is removed from them, but into accurate categories otherwise. Although existing models excel at detecting traditional static backdoors, we demonstrate that standard techniques fail to identify this type of backdoor when using widely adopted content-agnostic approaches. In contrast, we show that models trained on diverse, unchanging datasets can recognize a new type of backdoor we call "dynamic" that functions by targeting a specific target class after images are processed through a layer that calculates global averages, but misclassifies samples into accurate categories into any other category. Our research also explores multiple target configurations and training methods, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of the effects of the "dynamic" backdoor on model performance, which can be applied to create more realistic and actionable threats.

In our research, we delve into the intricate connection between general relativity and astrometry, focusing on how precise measurements of star movements in the sky can provide valuable insights into fundamental physical constants. We outline the principles of the Post-Newtonian formalism and explore how precise measurements of proper motions, combined with precise ephemerides, can yield a precise estimate of one of the key Post-Newtonian parameters, $\gamma$. The parameter $\gamma$ is a critical component of gravitational theory and has profound implications for gravitational effects on the movement of stars. In our analysis, we use the exceptional accuracy of the Gaia satellite to quantify the impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on the reliability of calculated distances to stars. The results of our research highlight the significant influence of $\gamma$ uncertainty on the reliability of distance measurements, particularly for distant objects. The objects with the most precise calculated distances are found to be unrelated to the Milky Way, such as globular clusters. We demonstrate the minimal impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on the reliability of distance measurements for objects within the Milky Way, such as exoplanets. The removal of $\gamma$ uncertainty leads to a slight improvement in the calculated distances for the majority of objects, while leading to a significant improvement for distant objects such as globular clusters. The objects with the most reliable calculated distances are found to be $\omega Centauri$ and M55.

Human intuition enables us to generate innovative ideas and anticipate unforeseen situations, surpassing human experience.  Ongoing research has focused on understanding the underlying basis of our everyday knowledge.  Question answering based on broad knowledge databases has become a significant challenge in artificial intelligence, necessitating an in-depth exploration of the structure and nature of our common knowledge.  Current methods tackle this issue by utilizing related questions to enhance model performance, however, this approach merely leverages this connection superficially, without delving into its underlying meaning.  In response to this limitation, a novel framework is introduced called SC2A, which utilizes a semantic matching module to identify questions with a strong semantic connection and a refinement module to combine the output of both careful and careless models.  This research also introduces a new dataset, called Commonsense Question Answering (CQA), which comprises 10,000 complex questions that require the utilization of domain knowledge to answer, along with a corresponding set of related questions.  When applied to this new dataset and two established benchmarks, the SC2A model achieves a notable improvement in performance compared to the current state-of-the-art, while demonstrating a strong semantic connection between the input questions and the answers they elicit.

Astronomical environments have been observed to contain molecular cations for decades. Although neutral molecules are more commonly known, these cations play a significant role in determining the properties of neutral species. Despite this, many potential molecular cation species have yet to be detected in space. A notable example is the absence of stable oxygen-containing molecular cations, with the possible exception of H2O2+ and CHO+, has been found so far. This scarcity is surprising given the prevalence of such compounds in space. This review examines the properties of potential comet spectra-forming molecular cations that contain oxygen, including HCO+, O+, and their more complex variants. It highlights areas where current knowledge falls short, particularly in the infrared wavelength range, and calls for a comprehensive investigation of molecular cation spectra to deepen our understanding of space formations.

In Federated Learning, the process of learning from decentralized devices involves exchanging data and models with a central server. A key challenge in this process is the variability of data samples across devices, known as Non-IID data, which can hinder the performance of the learning algorithm. Current methods to address this issue require altering the data or models, which may not be feasible in some situations. Our proposed approach, Stroll, utilizes random walk sampling to address this issue. By simulating a random stroll, the sum of gradient updates follows the same path as a single update from a balanced data distribution, which can significantly boost the performance of the learning process. Our study shows that Stroll outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods, achieving comparable results to an ideal scenario where the sum of updates is from a balanced data distribution.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health issues, and without proper treatment, these problems can worsen and increase the likelihood of reoffending. In an attempt to address this, a regulation in Italy mandates that certain convicted individuals undergo psychological assessment and, if necessary, pay for psychiatric or psychological therapy. This study examines the impact of such therapy on crime rates among these individuals, and it is found that being subjected to this therapy significantly increases the likelihood of committing another crime within three years. It is hypothesized that this effect is caused by the stress resulting from being forced to receive therapy, rather than the therapy itself providing benefits. It is also found that this three-year timeframe is marked by an increase in crimes, with the regulation having no discernible effect on crime rates beyond this period.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial step in many clinical applications.  Despite its significance, performing this task is often challenging due to limited data.  This issue is compounded in semi-supervised settings, where a mix of annotated and unannotated images is used for segmentation.  In these semi-supervised settings, models are prone to overfitting and producing inconsistent segmentations across similar unannotated images.  We present a consistency regularization technique called SIR that addresses this challenge by enforcing the segmentation of unannotated images to remain unchanged under identity augmentation.  When applied to the popular U-Net architecture in semi-supervised settings, our SIR method yields consistent results and improves performance in several semi-supervised medical image datasets, including mitosis, retinopathy, and eye disease segmentation.

To enhance our understanding of complex system dynamics, machine learning models, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), have been successfully applied. A key concern, however, is their lack of interpretability. In response, researchers have developed the Graph Attention Variational Attention Network (GAVAN) to provide a more transparent explanation of network attention mechanisms. GAVAN combines two attention mechanisms, variational attention networks and global GNN, to generate precise, actionable insights. When tested on diverse datasets, including the Lorenz system, GAVAN outperforms existing GNN models in both prediction accuracy and feature importance analysis. A comparative study with the traditional Newtonian approach further highlights the GAVAN's effectiveness in identifying key influencing factors in complex systems.

Consider a mixture distribution where the components are parametric, and the parameters follow some distribution. These models are commonly used in areas such as nonresponse weighting adjustments, latent variables, and item response theory. When data is available, estimating the distribution of parameters becomes crucial. This distribution can be effectively approximated using a finite mixture model with unknown parameters. In this study, we aim to estimate the parameters of these underlying models, and consequently, the quantities of interest can be calculated as functions of these parameters. We introduce a new Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator (GMLE) that estimates the quantity of interest directly, rather than the parameters individually. This GMLE is used to estimate proportions of a population in the context of sampling with latent variables. Simulation studies are conducted to compare the GMLE with other estimation methods.

Knowledge tracing has become a popular method to customize learning experiences by predicting students' mastery of concepts. Although neural network-based knowledge tracing methods have shown better performance compared to traditional approaches, evaluating and comparing different models has been made difficult due to the lack of unified standards and evaluation protocols. To address this challenge, we developed PyKT, a Python package that facilitates the fair and standardized assessment of deep learning-based models for knowledge tracing. PyKT includes reference implementations of popular models, standardized protocols for fair comparisons, and plotting tools for visualizing results. We demonstrate the utility of PyKT by evaluating several models on the C-MKTest dataset and providing the code for these evaluations. PyKT is an open-source package available on GitHub at https://github.com/HaibinZhang/pykt.

This paper proves that the elliptic operator L, which is a second-order differential operator, has a closed range on a vast class of non-compact manifolds M. These manifolds are equipped with a smooth measure $\mu$ and are such that any smooth, compactly supported vector field that preserves the measure must also be globally solvable. This result is significant because it implies that R, which represents the range of L, is precisely the set of functions on M that are orthogonal to its kernel. This discovery is particularly noteworthy in the context of various types of nonlinear transport equations, where it guarantees that R consists of functions on M that allow for a well-defined Leray solution to a given nonlinear transport equation.

Several proof assistants have developed specific formats for importing natural-deduction arguments, but these formats lack universality due to their specific logic and term structures. To address this limitation, we have created a genericSMT-based argument format that enables the integration of external arguments regardless of the proof assistant's specific term structure. By utilizing parsetree adapters, we can import arguments for proof assistants with complex term structures, such as Coq, Agda, and Lean. These arguments can then be utilized with existing technologies, including automatic proof completion and proof planning.

As Federated Learning (FL) expands into resource-constrained devices, clients' varying computing and communication capabilities create significant FL progress barriers. Although techniques to address this heterogeneity have been developed for FL, this problem presents unique challenges for FL. This work explores an unrestricted FL setting where FL clients can alter the FL model parameters freely, a dilemma further compounded by the asynchronous FL model aggregation barrier. In response to this challenge, the delayed FL model aggregation allows for a buffer to collect models from all FL devices before performing asynchronous model aggregation, thereby guaranteeing reliable participation of all FL devices while mitigating the impact of model distortion. This technique has been adapted to both distributed stochastic gradient descent and FL, yielding robust performance in the Asynchronous FL Buffering Learning problem.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have
incorporated character-level outputs to facilitate post-processing and enable
translations. However, this approach assumes that ASR and translation tasks
share the same input data, a limitation that excludes post-processing
capabilities for languages lacking high-quality training transcripts. To address
this challenge, a two-stage neural framework is proposed for cross-language ASR
transfer, a situation where the target language's transcript is unavailable. In
this novel setup, a target language keyword ASR model is trained to detect
prominent words by leveraging source language features and publicly available
text data. Subsequently, the most salient target language keywords are utilized
to train a more accurate, document-level source language translation model.
Empirical results on the IWSLT'18 French-to-English translation task demonstrate
that this method significantly surpasses baseline models, yielding a 14.44%
reduction in relative loss and a 4.0 BLEU score improvement.

Our novel TD learning method overcomes the main challenge of conventional
TPD algorithms, where the steady-state solution is elusive due to the need
for an infinite number of iterations.  In our approach, a Gaussian Process
model effectively models the sparse approximation of the control function,
utilizing regression techniques to calculate the TD error and update the GP
based on the Bellman equation.  This enables the robot to learn guidance
efficiently with limited data, avoiding the need for infinite iterations.
To further enhance performance, we incorporate sparsity constraints into our
model, enhancing both computational effectiveness and model interpretability.
We demonstrate the benefits of our approach through theoretical analysis
and numerical simulations, showcasing improved learning speed and
performance compared to conventional TPD algorithms.

We employ a anisotropic dual-fluid model to describe compound stellar objects, consisting of two distinct fluid spheres with potentially different radii, intertwned generalizations of the Barutini metric facilitate this two-fluid description. We derive a comprehensive set of field equations for anisotropic dual-fluid configurations, then focus on a specific intertwned Barutini metric. Radii continuity and matching boundary conditions at fluid interfaces provide four crucial constraints. We investigate single-fluid and one-small-inner-sphere scenarios as special cases, with the small-inner-sphere configuration serving as a relativistic model for dark star planets.

Most current SEC systems struggle to perform well on domains not seen during training, particularly when there's limited data available. This performance drop is caused by poor generalization to new domains. Current methods to enhance the SEc generalization capability involve data augmentation, but these approaches require either a large amount of labeled data or the same level of labeling as the original dataset. In contrast, our goal is to enable the SEC model to adapt to new domains with few examples, even when there's no access to parallel data. In this study, we investigate the domain adaptation problem in SEC and demonstrate that models pre-trained with a sequence-to-sequence approach are highly susceptible to domain shift issues. We further show that these models can be efficiently adapted to new domains using meta-learning, despite the potential for data leakage in the current multi-task setup. To address this, we propose a novel meta-learning framework that separates the training and testing data. We evaluate our approach on few-shot domain transfer tasks using the TED-LIUM 6 dataset and two other real-world SEC datasets. We also conduct ablation studies to better understand the model's behavior. We find that our model excels at few-shot domain transfer, outperforming strong baselines with as little as 10 examples per class, and achieving a 13.60/10.50/8.50 error rate reduction on single-/double-/triple-domain transfer tasks, respectively.

When allocating goods that cannot be divided among self-interested agents, it's essential to achieve two goals: ensuring the allocated goods are envy-free and acknowledging the agents' ability to act strategically. Our research makes a breakthrough by combining these aspects, ensuring algorithmically fair outcomes remains valid in the face of strategic behavior. Specifically, when agents can manipulate the system to maximize their utility, our results show that any outcome achieving a level of fairness known as Max-Min Fairness can be obtained, along with corresponding allocations that are robust and individually rational. Moreover, we also consider agents acting in a coalition, demonstrating that fair allocations can be achieved that are resistant to coalition formation.

UGC 8839 is an exceptional star-forming ring galaxy with a highly distorted foreground galaxy interacting with it. A remarkable feature of UGC 8839 is its exceptionally low level of global star formation activity, as evidenced by its low specific star formation rate and old stellar population, as indicated by its near-infrared color. A detailed analysis of its near-infrared image reveals a unusual, compact, and intensely red region at the center of the ring, characterized by a high column density and low dust extinction, suggesting a long-standing, quiescent star formation site. This enigmatic structure, dubbed the "hyper-stable disk," has persisted for an extended period, as indicated by its compact size and lack of significant stellar bursts, and may be attributed to the interaction between the two galaxies, potentially due to a tidal dwarf galaxy or a protected star-forming region. The discovery of this hyper-stable disk in UGC 8839 is a unique phenomenon that highlights the complex interplay of tidal interactions and star formation dynamics in ring galaxies.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of two-current correlations in pions was conducted, with quark bilinears representing either flavor or spin, along with meson bilinears as a reference. For light quarks, clear three distinct associations emerge: local, semi-local, and highly non-local, with their corresponding distances being approximately 0.5 fm, 1.5 fm, and beyond 2.0 fm, respectively. The results for the up and down quarks are nearly identical. The analysis also included the impact of varying quark masses, with results presented for both pions and rho mesons across a range of masses. The study further examined these associations at finite quark masses beyond the massless limit and beyond the physical region. In the latter case, the analysis of lattice data was complemented by effective field theory, specifically chiral perturbation theory, applied to the masses of meson bilinears.

As protostellar objects with disks undergo significant changes in their
accretion rates over time, this variability has important consequences
for planet formation. A notable aspect of this variability is long-term
oscillations observed in some objects, which may be key to explaining
accretion rate distribution. Our study focuses on XX Cha, a high-mass object
whose accretion rates can be significantly different from its peers by
multiple orders of magnitude. By analyzing its light curve, we found that
XX Cha exhibits an unusual, gentle oscillation with a ~1000-day period,
which may be comparable to other unique objects like HL Tau and DM Tau.
However, there are no current models that can explain the origin of these
long-period variability patterns seen in these objects. Without such models,
accretion rate distributions may not be reliable tools for understanding
accretion flow dynamics. Our research also found that the light variability
in XX Cha is not evenly spread across its disk, which may have implications
for the formation of planets, especially those located further from the star.
Our results indicate that large planets may have already been formed close
to the star and that smaller embryos are more likely to be found further
out. Our research also highlights the importance of studying light variability
in relation to planet formation.

In offline single-agent reinforcement learning, the assumption of invariant data distribution between state value and Q-function evaluations is often violated, leading to a significant challenge known as "double descent." This issue arises because the model evaluates the Q-function or value at a re-sampled action, which may not be available during the training data. Although this problem has been extensively studied in single-agent scenarios, there has been little exploration of its impact in the offline multi-agent reinforcement learning setting. In this paper, we investigate the offline multi-agent scenario under the assumption of independent and identical probabilistic actions. This analysis reveals that the "double descent" phenomenon also applies in this setting. Furthermore, we propose a novel method called GPS (Good Path Based) that leverages high-quality training samples to mitigate "double descent." Experimental results in both grid world and MuJoCo environments demonstrate that GPS significantly improves the performance of existing offline multi-agent algorithms by at least 10% and 60%, respectively.

Radiation therapy treatment planning relies on accurate patient anatomy alignment with 3D images, and while low-energy images like X-rays and CT scans provide this guidance, they lack the detail needed for large tumors. MV images, commonly used in radiation therapy, contain abundant information about tumor location but are limited in resolution. To compensate, we aim to accurately and automatically align small, irregular MV images with high-resolution reference images. Although image registration techniques exist, their application to radiographic images is challenging due to their sparse and noisy nature. In this study, we investigate the potential of convolutional neural networks to predict image displacements from radiographic inputs, comparing 2D and 3D MV image alignments. We also explore the use of super-resolution methods to generate higher-quality radiographic images before alignment. Our results show that directly aligning images using a neural network offers superior performance compared to improving image quality first, and that even low-quality 3D MV images can be accurately aligned with their corresponding images.

Quantum nonlocality manifests in two primary forms. While single-particle entanglement has been shown to lead to the nonlocal steering of a single particle, we demonstrate that entanglement can also result in a genuinely nonclassical, two-party steering scenario, distinguishing it from the classical two-party steering previously linked to Bell entanglement.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence technologies within Internet of Vehicles systems has been impeded by significant data privacy and security risks, particularly in scenarios involving centralized data aggregation and model training. A potential solution to this problem is the combination of Federated Learning and Blockchain technologies, which could facilitate decentralized model training while maintaining data privacy. However, a comprehensive research on this subject is lacking in the current body of knowledge. The purpose of this work is to fill this gap by conducting a systematic literature review on FL/BC learning frameworks for decentralized IOTV applications. The review covers and analyzes various aspects, including Decentralized FL architectures, Blockchain protocols, privacy protection protocols, and DL/FL models employed in IOTV scenarios. The results of this review are presented and discussed, providing insights and potential future research directions.

V392 Persei, a nova that occurred in 2012, stands out as a particularly luminous event among novae. V392 Persei exhibited extreme characteristics, including high X-ray and gamma-ray outputs, surpassing previous novae in these aspects. Observations from the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor revealed gamma-ray emissions during the nova's declining phase, with spectral analysis pointing to gamma-rays produced by electrons in the nova wind interacting with their own radiation field. V392 Persei's low mass ejection velocity of approximately 150 km/s, combined with its gamma-ray emissions, sets it apart from typical novae. Investigating the physical conditions of this event required studying V392 Persei's donor star, with observations from various instruments revealing the star to be a low-mass X-ray binary with a specific type of outburst pattern known as dwarf nova. The observed gamma-ray emissions from V392 Persei can be accounted for by interactions between the nova wind and the donor star, with estimates of the donor star's temperature and electron temperature derived from observational data.

A proposed downlink precoder selection method utilizes codebook search reduction and feedback encoding techniques. Initially, a lookup table is generated based on a Gaussian random field and a verified approach to create equivalent precoders from a codebook. Then, during a codebook search, feedback is encoded to find the codebook panel that best matches the desired precoder, and a code within that panel that best matches the desired precoder is selected. A step of feedback rounding is included to determine the final feedback. Numerical results show improved throughput for both single and multiple user scenarios in an LTE system.

We perform detailed, comprehensive, and three-dimensional nonequilibrium current density calculations and visualizations for the lowest energy, periodic, and spatially confined, periodic boundary-condition models of the 2D square lattice Hofstadter system under nonequilibrium conditions.

For stars, mass loss rates are commonly determined by examining the particles that escape from the outer layers of the star. In contrast, there is an existing limit on how quickly massive black holes can lose mass through radiation known as the Bondi limit. We propose a rate for the gravitational wave emission from gas accreting onto a massive black hole that can exceed the Bondi limit when the surrounding environment includes a radiatively efficient accretion disc. By equating the power generated by radiation and gravitational wave emission, we derived two limit conditions for a range of frequencies emanating from the outer regions of the accretion disc. These limit conditions depend on various factors, including the mass and spin of the black hole, as well as the properties of the accreted matter. As an example, we found that for a specific set of conditions, a $10^6 M_{\odot}$ black hole surrounded by an accretion disc can emit up to $10^{-4}$ bits of information per Planck time through gravitational waves.

The initial population of stars, which formed in the early universe's dark matter-halo protogalaxies, eventually congregated in the centers of these galaxies, creating dense star clusters that contained around 10 to 100 primordial black holes. We created a computational model to simulate the interactions and mergers of these black holes within these star clusters, using results from the early universe's particle collisions to inform our model. We found that the convergence of narrow mass distributions of these primordial black holes could significantly boost the early production of gravitational waves, increasing their amplitude by up to tenfold compared to previous estimates. This enhancement would be most pronounced in a specific frequency range, making these star clusters a promising source for detecting gravitational waves from the dawn of time with highly sensitive detectors like LISA and Einstein Telescope.

In this study, we analyze the physical layer security risks in an OFDM system with an intelligent wiretap relay. The system comprises two legitimate users, a public relay, and a wiretap receiver, all connected via distinct wireless links to an ideal full-duplex transmitter without self-interference. The transmission scheme involves sending an OFDM signal to the users through the relay. The users are capable of overhearing the direct transmission from the transmitter to them. We evaluate an end-to-end secrecy capacity formula and an average throughputs in this configuration. To improve throughput performance, we also examine the relationship between transmission rates and available system resources. In addition, we derive precise performance bounds in scenarios with limited or suboptimal wireless connections.

Text-based RPGs, popular in the late 20th century, are making a comeback, as seen with hits like Pokémon Go and Stardew Valley. Behind the scenes of these games, developers utilize text-based RPG simulators to test and refine millions of player moves. Our technology, TextWorld, offers a high-speed text-based RPG simulator that can execute one second's worth of gameplay equivalent to 500,000 to 800,000 individual actions, depending on the complexity of the game. This performance makes it feasible to play five million rounds of a text-based RPG in a single day. The Simulacrum testing platform, built using TextWorld, enables the evaluation of human-like decision-making strategies for moves the average player wouldn't consider, prompting the exploration of novel and unconventional gameplay methods.

Deep learning methods, particularly Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), have achieved significant success in video understanding tasks. However, their practical application is hindered by their slow processing speeds and excessive computational costs. To address these limitations, this study introduces an optimized RNN architecture called RNN-T, which replaces traditional RNN components with efficient Matrix Multiplication layers. By leveraging tensor decomposition, this design enables matrix-partitioning across tensor cores, resulting in a 2.8-fold increase in RNN performance and a 4.3-fold decrease in energy consumption when implemented on specialized hardware. Furthermore, a unique tensor allocation scheme is developed to handle varying RNN states and sizes, and an application-specific RNN-T accelerator is presented for video recognition tasks using hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition. Experimental results demonstrate that this system can process 100 seconds of video RNN processing with a 100 times greater speed and a 10 times lower energy consumption compared to current tensor-based RNN implementations on general-purpose processors.

The concept of gravity's weakness in certain regimes has led to the conjecture that operators with a specific convexity property, denoted as $\theta_n$, are also limited to a particular range. This paper aims to clarify the precise meaning of the convexity of these operators, denoted as $a_n$, by exploring its relationship with the moment problem. It is shown that the convexity of the distribution $a_n$ is intimately connected to the growth rate of the $n$-th derivative of a function $I_n$ at zero. This relationship allows us to establish the validity of a key principle, known as the "weak gravity conjecture", which states that there exists a power $p$ such that the magnitude of $I_n$ grows in proportion to $n!$ multiplied by $p^n$. This, in turn, is shown to be connected to the existence of a primary operator with a specific scaling dimension, denoted as $\Delta_{\text{lightest}}$, that is less than one. By combining this insight with existing results, it is shown that the inequality $\Delta_{\text{lightest}} < 1$ holds true.

We establish a primary characteristic to identify when the tightness of external powers of an $M$ holds, which in turn implies that positive answers to whether the tightness of the F-operation continues, and the f-rationality of local varieties, are inherently polynomial properties. This discovery enables us to confirm that these attributes are tied to the Hilbert polynomial of the relevant degree for an Eisenstein local ring, thereby implying that they are also inherent properties. Additionally, we explore the connection between the Hilbert function and polynomial of the relevant degree for the Senos decomposition of an arbitrary module.

The integration of auxiliary services in energy markets is an essential aspect of policy design for robust power systems. To enhance grid stability, auxiliary services compensate for potential disruptions by providing essential support. The cooperative nature of auxiliary services has not been fully explored in existing policy frameworks. Current procurement approaches, primarily based on price-cap contracts, motivate generators to overstate their auxiliary service requirements, potentially leading to unnecessary auxiliary service purchases. In response, this research introduces a declarative-based auxiliary services acquisition model that encourages truthful revelation of interactions and develops a centralised auxiliary services procurement mechanism. This mechanism, supported by tailored menu-based contracts, facilitates a feasible and efficient auxiliary services trading platform. A numerical example is presented to illustrate the practical application of the proposed mechanism.

Saturn's atmosphere is experiencing significant changes as its seasons shift. Observations from multiple sources, including the Cassini spacecraft, have revealed the formation of a strong polar vortex in the north during the summer months. This vortex is located within a six-sided pattern that encircles a region of high temperatures in the polar upper atmosphere. Unlike previous observations of polar vortexes on Saturn, this one has a very high temperature difference and has been present for an extended period of time. The formation of this polar vortex is linked to the breakdown of a temperature wave in the stratosphere and is unlike similar phenomena observed on other planets like Jupiter and Neptune during their springtime. Unlike previous polar vortexes on Saturn, this one has a distinct composition with different chemical components at different temperatures. The scientists believe that the polar vortex may be influenced by the movement of warm air from lower latitudes and that it may last for several months before disappearing.

A recent paper by Lerner and Vasy explores the Schrödinger equation outside a convex object, given by $ \partial_t u + \Delta u = 0 $ outside the object, with $ u $ vanishing on the object's surface. For any point inside the object, there is no delay in the spread of $ u $'s amplitude over time compared to an unrestricted spread in higher dimensions. This allows for the existence of solutions that explode with time, where the rate of explosion is bounded both above and below, given by $\Big(\frac{C_1}{t}\Big)^{\frac{n-\sigma}{2}} \leq |u| \leq \Big(\frac{C_2}{t}\Big)^{\frac{n-\sigma}{2}} $, with $\sigma$ representing the area of the object's surface relative to its total area. This result is analogous to a previous finding by Izzo, Morame, and Vasy for the Schrödinger equation with a potential, where $\sigma$ is given by $2$.

A local uniform embedding is considered a positive characteristic, finitely produced algebra variant of a local uniform presentation of an algebraic variety. This concept is used to examine the characteristics of varieties defined over a non-negative characteristic field, given a finite produced algebra. Specifically, we have established that for a variety constructed from a produced algebra in characteristic zero with positive characteristic, certain properties hold true. These properties include the fact that the variety can be defined through a set of homogeneous equations in a particular equation, and that the equation is effective and has a degree that is bounded. Additionally, the equation is valid for a variety that can be defined through a set of homogeneous equations in a particular equation, with a degree that is bounded. These bounds are all explicitly defined and depend on the characteristics of the algebra and the equation.

We create a symmetric monoidal category of graded bundle functors, identifying De Rham bundle as a notable example. Our work generalizes previous findings by Baez and Schreiber, who defined graded bundle higher presheaves, by defining these higher presheaves based on bundle degree sequences.

Let G be a reductive group defined over a field F. We introduce two notable constructions: G^{\sharp}, which is a modification of G that maintains the same reductive properties over F, and \mu_G, which is a function mapping smooth, compactly supported elements of orbital integrals to real numbers. This \mu_G function is shown to be compatible with the structure of G^{\sharp}, and it connects to the \mu introduced by Jia and Zhang in a previous study (arXiv:1809.00122) for the case where F is a local field. Notably, both \mu_G and \mu_{G^{\sharp}} are shown to be unnecessary in the context of the stable trace formula developed by Jia and Zhang, but they are shown to be essential in the work of Waldspurger for non-quasi-split groups. We demonstrate its necessity by utilizing Spinv_4 over a real quadratic field in our study.

Research into the nuclear giant dipole resonance through light scattering reveals details about the nuclear structure. A new method has been developed to analyze the radiation emitted by nuclei scattering photons, by examining the intensity of scattered x-rays in relation to the energy of the resonance. This technique enables traditional x-ray scattering techniques to provide new insights into the dynamic properties of nuclei. A theoretical framework has been established to interpret the data obtained using this technique, which can be applied to various types of scattering experiments involving weakly perturbed nuclei.

Our research develops finite element models to accurately simulate single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured, porous medium. Our approach uses hybrid-mixed methods, treating fracture permeability independently from the surrounding medium. Our framework is flexible enough to handle complex, curved fractures and provides robust, convergent solutions. Our approach yields post-computation solutions with a higher level of accuracy. Our method's efficiency and reliability are demonstrated through a range of examples.

Hypothesis evaluation is a fundamental aspect of science, and Bayes factors play a key role in comparing the support for two competing hypotheses. Despite their theoretical benefits, Bayes factors can behave erratically in practical applications, particularly in statistical studies. This research aims to map out the most successful approaches for employing Bayes factors in real-world scenarios. By combining elements of literature review and experimental analysis, we focus on various methods to address three frequent issues: assessing the null hypothesis, managing unexpected findings, and managing data that fall outside expected parameters. Our study compares different strategies, including conventional practices and less conventional approaches, to address these issues. Through a comprehensive set of 166 Bayesian ANOVA studies, we evaluate the impact of various approaches on the comparison between support for the null and alternative hypotheses. Our findings reveal that careful experimental design is of paramount importance, followed by the exclusion of unusual observations, and that more unconventional approaches can produce more consistent results than common practices. Ultimately, this research provides a solid foundation for further exploration of practical Bayes factor applications, including the development of standardized protocols for specific statistical techniques and the incorporation of simulation methods to anticipate the effects of unexpected or unusual data on Bayes factor outcomes.

This study introduces Discourse Sense, an innovative approach to assigning semantic values to discourse indicators based on their contextual usage. By treating indicators as words with distinct meanings, this research develops a novel method for contextual representation that combines one hundred and five established techniques, resulting in the creation of four specific indicator representations. Through rigorous evaluation with three major discourse indicators - however, therefore, and indeed - this research employs two performance metrics - contrastive human labeling and tripartite classification - to demonstrate the effectiveness of its examination. The results highlight the contextual nature of discourse indicators and the necessity for contextual examination methods, ultimately contributing a comprehensive dataset comprising one hundred and ten thousand labeled examples to facilitate further investigation.

From the perspective of global optimization, we investigate the geodesic convexity of nonconvex matrix decompositions. Our primary contribution is a comprehensive framework that explains why nonconvex matrix decompositions exhibit geodesic convexity, providing implications for a range of low-rank matrix optimization problems. By analyzing specific examples, including nuclear norm regularization and robust matrix completion, we demonstrate how the loss landscape of these methods is geodesically convex within a particular region of the ambient space. This region is defined by a specific configuration of singular values that correspond to the singular values of the target solution. Within this region, the loss landscape is shown to be strictly convex with a positive-definite Hessian at any point, where the geometry of the underlying manifold is determined by the arrangement of the solution's subspace relative to the ambient space. Our work offers a novel approach to understanding the geometric properties of nonconvex matrix decompositions and their implications for low-rank matrix optimization.

In 1983, Goldberg and Seymour proposed the conjecture that for any bipartite graph G with no multi-edge, if the sum of the degrees of any two distinct vertices is less than five times the sum of the degrees in two other specific graphs, then G can be edge-colored in a way that uses at most 3 more colors than its chromatic index.

We investigate how populations of players with varying strategies in a repeated Cournot market reach a balance between individual success and collective stability. Using genetic algorithms to explore the parameter space, we examine two populations interacting across two markets and four identical populations in a single market. Our results highlight three key findings: first, mutualism emerges in the two-population scenario, leading to greater success for both groups; second, a single population can display cooperative or non-cooperative behavior depending on initial conditions in the same market; third, periodic or chaotic dynamics arise from interactions among players. Our research offers insight into the conditions under which genetic algorithms can facilitate cooperative behavior and promote long-term sustainability.

For any positive integer s, we define typical edge ideals and typical symbolic edge ideals of weighted oriented graphs. Initially proposed by Harbourne and Van Tuyl, these concepts extend the typical properties of primary decompositions. We establish key relationships between the typical symbolic and typical primary components, demonstrating that the typical symbolic powers equate to the typical primary powers. Building on work by Dao, Nguyen, and Van Tuyl, we determine that the typical symbolic and typical primary powers of these ideals consist of extensions of some of their own. Moreover, for tree DAGs, we prove that the typical symbolic and typical primary powers of ideals have the same composed structure as their symbolic and primary ones.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) excel in image classification tasks, surpassing humans in accuracy. Yet, their reliability is compromised by susceptibility to hardware malfunctions, which can cause incorrect outputs. This issue is critical for real-world applications of CNNs embedded in hardware systems, where component failures could lead to adverse consequences. This research proposes a framework to validate the safety of such systems by establishing bounds within which CNN activations remain, even in the event of hardware errors. By focusing on these activation ranges, this work aims to make progress toward guaranteeing that system outputs stay acceptable, a crucial step toward achieving that goal. This paper also presents initial findings demonstrating the effectiveness of enforcing these activation bounds using range supervision and fault injection testing, highlighting the need for continuous improvement in this area.

The original Jordanian twist quantization rule fails to fully characterize the R-matrix, leaving unspecified R-matrix components that could theoretically be infinite R-powsers series. This paper investigates this ambiguity by systematically examining R-matrix components across various scenarios. By defining specific subspaces where R-matrix coefficients reside, two distinct one-parameter R-matrix series configurations are identified. Consequently, two refined, parameter-based Jordanian twist definitions are proposed.

We introduce a novel approach to establish a unified vocabulary across multiple languages without utilizing parallel texts. By leveraging monolingual embeddings, we construct a common space where words from different languages can be effectively matched based on their intrinsic properties. A key aspect of this method is ensuring that the relationship between an individual word and its cluster remains consistent across various languages. This is achieved by optimizing a multi-language cluster-consistent word embedding model, taking into account both the intrinsic characteristics of each word's cluster and their inter-cluster connections. Experimental evaluations on five distinct tasks using data from three languages demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in creating a meaningful, interoperable space across languages without relying on any multilingual information.

This study presents first measurements of light-flavor pion, kaon, and proton production in 54 TeV Xe-Xe collisions, along with corresponding $p_T$-dependent nuclear modification factors and collective flow coefficients for these particles and for rare $\phi$ mesons.

In late October 2019, Chile experienced widespread unrest fueled by public discontent over government policies, the metro incident that triggered it, and a history of inequality and corruption. This study simulates the spread of these protests using a mathematical model based on a non-local version of the Susceptible, Susceptible, Infected, Removed framework. Distinct from traditional models, our approach incorporates spatial dynamics and varying levels of susceptibility among different populations. By comparing model predictions with actual data, we found a strong correlation between simulated and reported protest frequencies across various districts. Furthermore, visualizing the simulated unrest's temporal evolution reveals a high degree of accuracy in capturing the protests' spatial dynamics. Our model offers valuable insights into the 2019 protests and demonstrates the applicability of non-local epidemiological models to other spreading phenomena.

This research focuses on creating a solver for bare and expanded regular expression
constrains, classified as $r_1 \wedge r_2 \wedge \ldots \wedge r_n \wedge \overline{r_1} \wedge \overline{r_2} \wedge \ldots \wedge \overline{r_n} = \emptyset$,
where the letters within the (JEP) regular expressions are disjoint sets. By utilizing
the JEP characteristic that allows for the separate computation of complement
automata, we can efficiently compute the union of these automata. The result is a
DXN ABRACADABRA input format, which can be solved using an existing JEP-specific
2-CEGIS approach. The resulting solver is available as a JEP-autocorrector for
brarexpressions. The code is also extensible for non-disjoint sets of letters.

Our new approach, EMA-VIO, integrates an external memory attention mechanism into a deep visual-inertial localization network. This allows the system to effectively combine inertial data with a learned scene structure for accurate pose estimation. EMA-VIO uses external memory units to store frequency-specific information, which is then used to filter out noise from IMU data and predict future state based on the timing of the estimation. Experiments show that our system achieves highly precise performance, outperforming the current best time-domain end-to-end VIO method by a significant margin.

The concept of effective linear physics has been applied to various higher-order material systems, but our research introduces Weyl material models derived from a quartic Hamiltonian that can potentially be realized experimentally. In this study, we first analyze and classify different higher-order Weyl Hamiltonians mathematically, identifying various types of quadrupatic and quatic behavior. Then, we investigate the conditions under which specific material models display only quatic dominance or a combination of quartic and quadrupatic dominance. Our study reveals the rich topological characteristics of these higher-order Weyl phases, including higher-order and quadrupatic polarizations, as well as novel phase transitions. Finally, we investigate the response of material particles to external perturbations and demonstrate that certain higher-order Weyl phases exhibit square-root higher-order dynamics, effectively mimicking simpler two- or four-protective material behaviors.

This study investigates the reconstruction of missing boundary data for the source-free Maxwell's equations. A numerical quasi-reversibility method is used to resolve this problem, with convergence rates established for both H(curl) and L2 norms. The algorithm's stability and convergence are demonstrated numerically, showcasing the method's effectiveness in recovering data from boundary curves and surfaces.

The expanding pace of large language models necessitates a significant amount
of computational power and knowledge, posing a challenge for individual
institutions. To address this limitation, researchers have developed methods
for knowledge sharing among decentralized devices. However, existing
protocols struggle with inefficient communication, security risks, knowledge
manipulation, and coordination issues. To overcome these obstacles, we
proposed a novel decentralized knowledge sharing system called Federated
Selective Collection (FSC). FSC enables knowledge contributors to share high
quality data by filtering out low relevance content, effectively preventing
noise and manipulation. The protocol employs a novel reputation system to
assess the trustworthiness of knowledge contributors, and utilizes a
blockchain to securely store and verify shared knowledge. To facilitate
coordination and prevent coordination failures, we leveraged the benefits of
knowledge aggregation techniques. To illustrate the effectiveness of FSC, we
developed a proof-of-concept implementation for knowledge sharing among
educational institutions, utilizing an educational knowledge base.

It has been proven that if the Galois group of an abelian quartic field over the rational numbers is isomorphic to the symmetric group S4 or the alternating group A4, then there exists an elliptic curve whose 3-ramified property holds and whose Galois action on torsion fields results in this quartic field. Furthermore, this paper provides Galois-theoretic insights into purely imaginary quartic fields containing R23.
